utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. The usher probably is bringing in the witness. I will take advantage of these few seconds. May I tell you that we have now decided how to go about a different case, so therefore we are -- if you don't mind, we will change our plans and we would like to announce to you what our plans are for the future weeks. Now, we are going to sit the whole of next week except for Monday afternoon. This has already been agreed to. Now, the whole of the week of the 7th will be off, not only Monday and Tuesday, but from the 7th to the 11th plus Monday, the 14th of September. So there will be a week off plus Monday, the 14th of September. We will resume on the 15th of September...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: ... of that week, then the week of the 21st of September, the week of the 28th for three days, 28th, 29th, 30th. The 1st and the 2nd of October will be off. If the Prosecution has not finished their case, we will go on until the 9th of October. I hope that by the 9th of October, the Prosecution case will be finished, and at that stage, the Defence will probably have one, two weeks, two, three weeks, two weeks would be better, to prepare their case, so we would skip two or three weeks. If they want to have three weeks, it's a pity, because then on the 2nd of November, we have a Plenary Session of our Tribunal, so we would also have to skip that week, so we would have to have four weeks off and resume on the 9th of November. If the Defence could start again on the 26th of October, it would be probably better. Then we could have a break on the 2nd and 3rd and 4th of November and then start again on the 9th of November for as many weeks as are needed by the Defence. As I say, what is important is that we hope that by the 9th of October, at the latest, the Prosecution will have completed their case. So therefore, as I say again, the week of the 7th, the whole week will be off, including the following Monday, the 14th, and we would resume on the 15th of September and go on until the end, except for the 1st and the 2nd of October. All right? Let me now turn to Mr. Pavkovic and ask how many Defence counsel would like to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The cross-examination of attorney Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac will continue first. After her, attorney Luka Susak, followed by attorney Ranko Radovic, Petar Puliselic. Virtually all Defence counsel will cross-examine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about you then?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I said virtually all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thereby opening the possibility for me to join in as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Before Mrs. Glumac resumes cross-examination, may I ask all Defence counsel, bearing in mind the age of the witness and, of course, try to refrain -- refrain, I will not say "try," refrain from harassing the witness. Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I should like to continue where we broke off yesterday. All I have left are a few final questions. Yesterday, we were discussing the four statements that you made previous to coming to the Tribunal. Did you make this statement to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the presidency, the State Commission for the Collection of Data on War Crimes in the Territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? This was immediately following the events on the 2nd of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, did you make a statement to the investigating magistrate in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, did you make these two statements to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal on two occasions, from the 4th to the 10th of March, '98, and the 23rd of October, 1994; that is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you agree, when you look through these materials, you never previously mentioned this group of soldiers that came with Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, not once did you mention that they wore any kind of ribbons on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: What are ribbons?

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Strips.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But we don't find any mention of that in the four statements that you made.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: If I didn't mention them, nobody asked me about them.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Fine. You mention them for the first time here during the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: It should have been in the previous statements too.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you didn't say that the soldiers that you saw near your house had green and yellow ribbons.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I didn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you did mention it in your earlier statement in '98. Did you perhaps confuse the people who were wearing these ribbons?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you recall that subsequently, later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac, I'm so sorry to interrupt you, but could you please slow down and wait a few seconds after the answer of the witness so that we can get the translation? Otherwise, the transcript will not reflect what is said here in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't remember that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Every time you signed these statements, I will read out what is said to you at the end of your statements: "You are making a written statement saying that you have read the statement, that you agree with its contents, and that you confirm that by your signature."

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: The first statement, that one, I didn't read.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But it says that you did read it and you signed it. Who signed instead of you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He introduced himself as a journalist. That was the first statement.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But it was an official statement taken by official bodies with your signature.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I told you how I made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to the event itself. Can you tell us when the shooting started, the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How early? Can you define that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: About 5.00 or 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was it still dark?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Pitch dark?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: When the shooting started, it was still pitch dark.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said it was raining. Was there a mist?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Then, at the beginning, the rain didn't start immediately. Later on, when it began to dawn, the rain started.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you reached Jozo Alilovic, was it raining there?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One more question. Did either of your brothers work in the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes, one of them. The older one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I only have a couple of questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether the lights were on when you woke up in the house in which you were sleeping?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And who put the lights on?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: My sister did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: She had got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Were the lights on when you woke up?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Why didn't you switch it off if it was light?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: We did switch it off as soon as we got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was it daylight when you switched off the light, or did you switch it off out of fear?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: We switched it off because the bullets were falling into the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was it still a little dark?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When did your father come home on the 15th, that is, the eve of the event?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All day?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he go from home at all on the 15th? Did he attend any meeting where war and peace were discussed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you jumped off the balcony.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How high up is the balcony in relation to the ground?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Three, three and a half metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Three and a half metres. Were you hurt when you jumped?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was your father a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said yesterday that he was not armed.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he put away his weapon somewhere else and not in the house?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was he issued any weapon at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know Nedzad Dzidic and Muharem?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And Ibrica Karic?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I think I do, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was he hurt on the 16th of April? Do you know that he was hurt on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: One more question. Do you know whether there were village patrols in your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did they patrol the village?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I know there was guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was this guard duty kept regularly?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Susak. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I shall be brief today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to focus on your first statement made to the State Commission for the Collection of Data on War Crimes in the Territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When the man who questioned you arrived, did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did he say? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I don't remember the name. I was there in a large hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What did he say? What was the purpose of his questioning?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Just a statement. He didn't say anything about collecting data.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But he must have told you why he was asking for a statement from you.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: As a journalist, I think, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So he introduced himself as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he warn you that anything you say must be true?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: He did caution you about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that he wrote the statement himself.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you read that statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But he read out the contents of what he had written?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So he neither read out the contents nor did you read it yourself?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were questioned by the investigating magistrate, did he tell you that you shouldn't answer his questions only but that you must tell everything you know, that you mustn't gloss over anything, and that you must tell the truth? Did the judge tell you that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He did warn me that I had to tell the truth, but he didn't say that I didn't just have to answer his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But did he say that you mustn't keep silent over something that you know?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How then did you answer my learned friend Glumac's question regarding those ribbons by saying that you didn't say anything about them because nobody asked you about them and the judge had told you that you mustn't keep silent about anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I didn't think it was so important. Yesterday she wanted me to describe those soldiers in greater detail, and I didn't mention those patches at first, but when she asked me about those insignia, I explained in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So when you were talking to the magistrate, you said all you knew but what you considered to be important, so you yourself judged what was important and what was not?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No. The judge was asking me questions and I answered them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But didn't you freely tell your story at first before the magistrate? In the investigating stage, the procedure is different than it is here.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: But he also put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But didn't you start the story on your own first?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I started talking and then he would put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you follow the dictation of your statement that was being made when you were with the judge?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When the judge was dictating to the typist.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: The person who questioned me, he also typed, he was also typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: A woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But was somebody typing in addition to that woman? In the minutes, it says that the clerk was Amira Hasanica?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: That was the lady who was questioning me and she wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to make breaks, please, in between questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Radovic. The interpreters again have asked me to ask you to make a break, to wait a few seconds after getting the response, an answer from the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before signing, did you read the statement or did you say that you had listened to the dictation and so you didn't need to sign it?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for any compensation or damages when talking to the investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had been damaged and that you would ask for compensation of damages from the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you describe, when you were questioned by the investigators of the International Tribunal and when you mentioned the Kupreskic brothers, Zoran and Mirjan, were there photographs shown to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were you required to describe them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You could say one was good looking. The other was ugly. One had thinning hair, the other didn't.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't ask you to describe them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No. Some photographs were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When were photographs shown to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yesterday or the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Were the photographs shown to you before you came to the Tribunal to identify the Kupreskic brothers?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So before you identified them, just prior to the identification, you were shown their photographs; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. Mr. Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not understand the meaning of that last question put to the witness which was answered in the affirmative. Could Mr. Radovic please specify or clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I was absolutely precise. I asked the witness whether he was shown a photograph of either Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic before. His answer was no, but that those photographs were shown to him just prior to the hearing and before he identified the accused in the courtroom. And even then, he wasn't correct in pointing to Zoran and Mirjan. He pointed to the two brothers together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I may be wrong, but I can't check on the transcript, I'm afraid, because it's too late to see what the answer of the witness was about the photographs. Mr. Radovic just said that the photographs were shown to the witness here in The Hague just prior to the hearing. That is what you said. Did you get it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, is it right that the witness was shown the photographs, as he said, before giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, indeed. That is why I was asking about the meaning of that question. Because after the witness, in the context of the interviews we had with him, mentioned the presence -- as he has done during his previous written statement, the sequence of events at the place on the 16th of April and the presence of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, we also showed him pictures of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic. But that was after he had named those two persons that we showed him those photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Was that, indeed, in the month of March of that year or was that just before the hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, that is before arriving in The Hague, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, from the testimony of the witness, it is quite clear that never before coming to the court were the photographs shown to him, and I think that the witness was clear in that respect. But before he testified here in court, I had absolutely no contact with the witness to be able to suggest any answer that he may have given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Witness C, in answer to a question by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, as to the name of Dragan Papic's brother, you said his name was Goran or Zoran, so you don't know exactly, which is quite acceptable. However, I wanted to point out that in Ahmici, there are a number of persons with the surname Papic. Similarly, there is a person called Goran Papic, and there is another person called Zoran Papic. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. I'm sorry, the witness's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I pointed out that it was Dragan Papic's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes, you said that. I'm just noting it. I'm not objecting in any sense. Could you describe to us what that person that you claim is Dragan Papic's brother looks like? Tell us how tall he is, the colour of his hair, how old he is, roughly. Just describe him, if you can, so that we can check if it is the right person.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He's about 180 or 190 centimetres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How old was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Well, about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: The colour of his hair?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Fair, fair, like brown, golden brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigator on the 10th of March, 1998, you said that two or three days after the attack, while you were staying in Jozo's house, Ivo Papic arrived?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And that he asked Jozo to help him bury some Croats?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: No, he didn't ask him. He came to collect him and took him to bury somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But he said that they were going to bury Croats?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He didn't say Croats. He said that they were going to bury someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But you said that in the statement. You said that he had said that he wanted him to help him to bury some Croats. That is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He said that he wanted him to help him to bury somebody, and when Jozo returned, he said that he went to the cemetery to bury a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: When did Ivo come to Jozo's place?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: About midday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: When did Ivo return? When did Jozo return?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: In the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you again that you clearly stated that these were Croats. We have the statement here. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: It was Croats, but he didn't say on that occasion that -- Ivo didn't say, "We're going to bury Croats," but they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic, are you going to cross-examine the witness or can we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I wonder whether the Prosecutor would like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President, a few questions which will be as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, during the trial yesterday, you indicated in this room Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic without being able to give their first names. I would like for you to indicate to this Tribunal how you knew at that time the Kupreskic brothers, Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, and in what circumstances did you know them before the 16th of April, 1993? When did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I knew them. I went up to their neighbourhood. They were in the neighbourhood. It's not far from our house where they lived. It's about 300, 400 metres away. That's how. Zoran would come to my house as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The person that you designated as Zoran Kupreskic, would he come often to your house?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why would he come? Why would he come to your house?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Well, he would come with my older brother, with Senus, about a pullover or something like that that my mother was knitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you saying then that your mother was knitting a sweater for Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I can't recall very well whether she was knitting it for him, but he would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, you were interviewed on the 2nd of May, 1993 by an official from the Centre for the War Crimes and Genocide. Do you recall the circumstances under which this meeting took place? Where was it located? How long did it take? Who were the persons who asked questions and how long did you answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Well, that was in a hall. There were about 60 to 100 persons there in that hall. He came in as a journalist. Prior to my statements, other persons made statements, and he asked me a few questions, and that lasted about ten minutes to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it accurate to say that during that interview of 2nd May, 1993, you named, among other names, the names of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic as having been seen by you as soldiers on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it, indeed, true, that in his statement that we are speaking of now that was taken on the 2nd of May, 1993, that you named, among others, Mirjan Kupreskic and Zoran Kupreskic as soldiers that you saw on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were then interviewed on the 2nd of December, 1993 by an examining magistrate from Zenica. Is it, indeed, true on that date you also named, among others, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic as soldiers on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now let us move for a moment to what happened on the morning of the 16th of April when your brother was brought by a soldier, after jumping from the first floor balcony, and then you heard this gunfire. Now, for everything to be clear, could you first describe as clearly as possible how your brother was dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He had a black vest. I think he also had a Texas jean jacket on and jeans. He was wearing jeans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How, at that time, were you dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I had a light blue T-shirt, a dark lower part of a sweat suit which was dark blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In order to complete the information we have, can you please describe what took place that morning with your father?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: When we started hearing the shots, he started coming back from the mosque home, because we were locked, and he wanted to unlock us. He came to Zahir Ahmic, the neighbour's house. There were some soldiers at that house who told him, "Come here." He tried to flee, and then they hurt him in his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you please say what happened to your older brother? I'm not speaking of the one who was killed on the 16th of April, 1993, but your older brother whose name you will not give, but whom you will simply refer to as your older brother. Will you please tell this Tribunal what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: My older brother?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, the oldest in the family.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Well, he was killed on the front-line somewhere near Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with this: The two brothers who you knew, the Kupreskics, can you give us an idea of how long you had known them in April of the year we're dealing with? How long had you known them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: The 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, before then.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I had known them -- well, I had known them for eight years. That's how much I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Had you ever spoken to them yourself? Had you talked to them?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Zoran, you had spoken to him, had you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes. You know, at school or during summer recess, we would play soccer, all of us, and that's where we would meet most frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And his brother, did you meet him too and talk to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes, I would meet him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have one or two minor questions. I am afraid I was unable to check the transcript of yesterday's hearing. I can't remember what you said about the place where you were with Tomo when you saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic enter the house of Jozo. Were you in a yard or a few metres from that house, Jozo's house, or were you in a different house?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I was in the house, in another house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, so I was right then. Could you pick up Prosecution Exhibit 68? I wonder whether the registrar could be so kind as to give the witness Prosecution Exhibit 68. Could you please indicate to us on that exhibit where this house is located?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps we should go to closed session because, indeed, that was shown in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness D. May I ask you to read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will issue a folded piece of paper to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 72, Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, you are here benefiting from protection measures. I'm now going to ask you a number of questions and ask that you not give any names or identifying information. If we wish for the Tribunal to receive more detailed information, we would then go to closed session. You are here in a protected environment. You may answer questions in a very serene environment with security. May I first ask you to give the composition of your family?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I had five sons and a husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In 1993, how old were your children?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: My oldest was born in 1964, the second child in 1966, the third in 1972, the fourth in 1973, and the fifth in 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, I understand you've always -- well, you currently live in Ahmici or you've always lived in Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In which neighbourhood of Ahmici was your house located?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: In the lower part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, could you please talk to us about the time period preceding the 16th of April, 1993, from the end of the month of September or October 1992 until April 1993, and tell us what your relations were with your neighbours, in particular with the Croat residents of Ahmici, did you have any difficulties, and do you know whether or not other persons, other Muslims like yourself, encountered any difficulties during that time period?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Of course, they did. Especially we in the lower part of Ahmici, we were in very great danger, the people closer to the road, in particular, so that there would be an incident almost daily. They would insult us. If they meet a woman wearing pantaloons, they would say, "You balija woman." I didn't have any contact with men. He would come by in the car and shout, "We will not have pantaloons walking here." They would call out "Balijas." In the evening, we would be sitting together, then they would throw grenades into our meadows. The people closer to the road would have their windows broken. We were sorrowful. We didn't know what was happening. And so on, it went on like that. We saw that relations were not what they used to be. Before, we would exchange visits, and then suddenly, they somehow separated. They were doing something in secret. We didn't know what they were doing. But we saw that things were not what they used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did things change?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: In '92, things had changed. When our people went to Visoko, from then on, relations were not the same. We didn't exchange visits, or very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Before that change, did Croat neighbours have friendly relationships with you?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We visited those who were nearby. This was a great shock for us. We were nice with each other, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you name the Croat neighbours with whom you had friendly relations before the change?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I can. First the Papics, then we would visit the Kupreskics too. When Vlatko Kupreskic was operated (sic), he was small. We went there before too. But especially then, we visited his mother and Zoran's mother, and she would come to visit us too and everything was just fine. Then the Vidovics too. There were never any problems between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you describe in detail the problems you had, for example, with the neighbours that you just named and the closest Croat neighbours in particular? What type of problems in particular did you have with those people and what type of events occurred?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Well, let me see. We were in jeopardy. When incidents started in Nadioci and people were chased out, they came to complain that they were coming in the evening to intimidate them with socks over their heads. In the Bungalow, there were some troops there. We don't know. But our men went there too, and I personally saw them coming and going very frequently. We saw that something was wrong, that they didn't want to work with our people; they worked separately. Then it started at Nadioci and people came from there, telling us and crying about it. There was a small -- there was a village with a few Muslims there, and they would -- Salkic. What's his name now? Eso's father. I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to that family, the Salkic family, in Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Of course, I remember. At the time, there were just provocations, and then suddenly, I was spending the night with a relative because we were in danger, so often I would go up there. The army would pass. I was close to the road and I was afraid. So I would go and spend the night in the upper village. One morning, I met his father just below the upper mosque crying, saying what had happened. And he said, "They've killed my Eso, and I'm carrying him to do the religious rites prior to burial in the upper mosque." I didn't talk with him at any length. I hurried home. I saw that everything had turned out upside down. I went to see what had happened to my house, and then -- I can't remember his father's name, Cerimic, he would also come crying, saying that something was wrong, that they were working for themselves and that they were provoking them. Then Nail Ahmic would come and his wife. They abandoned their own home because of these provocations. All of this was happening near my house. They also demolished the house of Amila. She was in Australia. She would also come and tell us about these things. This was a terrible surprise for all of us, that it should come from our neighbours, because before that, we had good relations. The same happened in Nadioci and with us. They too used to live together well and exchange visits as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This man that you met that mentioned the death of his son stating that he was killed, that they killed him, who was he referring to? Who were "they"?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Eso. He said, "My neighbours killed my Eso." They planted some explosives. I don't understand anything about that. And that he was in a couple of pieces. I didn't look, but he just told me that, and he was crying. He headed towards the mosque and I went homewards, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you recall other events during that time period in which people that you knew, Muslims, were victims?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: This went on like this, provocation after provocation, and -- when was it? I think the 20th of October, we didn't stay at home because I personally experienced something that I thought I would never survive. My house was burnt, my car was torched, everything I had around the house. The ground floor was set on fire. They took my man, my husband. They beat him up. He returned, begging them to let the cows out, and the commander at the time from Nadioci was somebody in their army, and they beat him up. He couldn't move. He had to lie down. And that is when we abandoned our village. After a day or two, my neighbour told me that my cows were wandering in the roads. I came with my brother-in-law. I picked up my girl from the school. My house was at the end of the village. And I went in to pick up some clothing because I was in Vrhovine; I didn't have anything to wear. When I entered the house, everything was black on the ground floor and upstairs it was charred. One room was still on fire. Two men were looking after my house. They were from Nadioci. He wore a black beret on his head, and they looked after my house and they told us to come back, that they wouldn't hurt us. He said that we should go back but that we should surrender our weapons. I didn't discuss this with him. My sister-in-law said that if we had some, we would have surrendered, and if we had had weapons, then this wouldn't have happened. So I collected what I needed and what I could carry and I took my cows towards Vrhovine. After that, I went back again, about 20 days later. I first went to see one sister in the upper village. I stayed there for a while because my house was burnt. Then I visited with my other sister. When I gained a bit of courage, I would work during the daytime and spend the night up there. But the provocations continued. If it was fine during the day, in the evening they would start shooting again, and then cars would go by and they would insult us. There were people, displaced people, from Jajce. They came to stay with us, and they looted their homes. This went on until the 16th of April. I too would leave my house and stay in the weekend home of Dzambeg, and then the people around me, I would stay during the night, and then during the day, I would work in the fields. I didn't even have electricity. And that's how it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, for some clarification about your relations. You stated a moment ago that your husband was beaten by soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember why these soldiers would have done such a thing?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: He had come back to release the cows. We

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: came in. He was killed after the 16th of April. He said, "Halid is killed. Get out. There are none of our people around. You must leave the house." And he dragged me out of the basement. So my husband and I came out. He saw that the stable was on fire, so he went back to release the cow. This young man caught him, a young man, 20-year-old, he threw him to the ground and kicked him as much as he could. He broke his nose. It is still crooked as a result. That's what happened. The reason was that he went to release the cows and then he was really on his way up to the upper village. That's as much as I know. I don't know anything more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Again, for clarification about your account, all of this took place from the 20th of October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: All this was happening prior to the 16th of April. I can't really remember all the details. These were things that we experienced until the 16th of April. I didn't know that this would happen so as to take note of the dates and the events and the order in which they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, a moment ago you talked about the Papic family as being neighbours, Croat neighbours, with whom you had excellent relations, or at least friendly relations, while stating also that these relations at one moment then transformed. Do you recall what was the behaviour or the attitude that Dragan Papic had, the son of Papic?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: Dragan Papic knows everything. Let him take on his soul. Let him swear on the life of his son because he knows who killed our men, and all these other neighbours of ours that have been accused because they did everything in gloves. They pretended. They know what happened to so many of our people, so many innocent victims, so many orphaned children. If we had had anything, then this would not have happened to us. That's all I can say. And he knows everything. He went to the Bungalow. They had soldiers there who would gather every day. They did bad things at night. The next day, they would be singing and drinking and rejoicing, and we were all very sad because we didn't know what to expect for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we now go into closed session? I would like to show a number of documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, we are now in open session once again; therefore, I would ask that you not give any names or any identifying information. A moment ago, you mentioned Dragan Papic. You stated that you would see him going to the Bungalow. Do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: That depended. As he felt -- he did whatever he wanted. He walked around in all kinds of clothes. He would black himself and his wife in black walking (sic). He would frighten people, provoke people. He would pick up a rifle. (redacted) (redacted) and he came with his gun, and I asked him why he was carrying a gun, and he said, "There was a deer with a broken leg; I want to kill him." And he would provoke in this way. He was full of himself. Before, when we met, we were good neighbours. We never quarrelled or anything like that. I was crossing the road from Dzemila Ahmic. It was Ramadan. We were having a religious meeting, having dinner, and he went off to the Bungalow, and I found it strange. This was just before nightfall. Maybe it was night-time already. So I personally met him. He didn't say anything to me. He passed by me. I'm older, so he should say hello, but he didn't say anything. I had two meadows there. I could see him when I was working in the field and I could see him from my balcony too. I could see him going there often.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, do you see in this room the man you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I do. He has a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us where he is located?

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: I can. Near the door over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Madam, I would now like for you to explain to this Tribunal what happened on the 16th of April, according to your own memory, and with the words that are your own.

utterances.speaker: Witness C.
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, in the morning, I was in my own house. I wasn't sleeping. I, my daughter, and my husband got up. My husband went to the mosque and we got up to pray, and my daughter was getting ready to go. She put on a blue sweater. I remember well. She put a scarf on her head. And she didn't go. He went out and locked the door. He couldn't wait, he didn't want to be late, so she didn't go. So I was praying to God. I put the water on for the coffee. Then a bullet whizzed by my head and hit against the stove. She was still where she was before. Then there was another bullet that hit the cupboard. She sat down. I realised that something was happening,(redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What about the open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are we bringing up the blinds?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: He has a facial distortion, but it is transmitted in the lobby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. I understand it is public, but because of the facial distortion, we have to keep the blinds down. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Ahmic Fahrudin, born on the 8th of November, 1953 in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, you have requested face protection, and that has been granted. So you may testify here in all confidence that that protection measure has, in fact, been granted to you. Mr. Ahmic, could you tell us, up until 1993, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I lived in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How long did you live in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Since my birth until 1993, when I was expelled from there. Except in between, I worked in Rijeka for three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Essentially, you were a life-long resident of the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I always lived in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us how much education you've had?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I have completed eight years of education. I work in the Zenica ironworks as a highly skilled worker in metallurgy, in the coke crushing plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you work there now at the Zenica steel mill?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I still work in the steel factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said you lived in Ahmici for all of your life. Did you live in the same house in Ahmici all your life or did you have different homes?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I lived with my parents until I built a new house for myself. I used the land and I built a new house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What part of Ahmici did your parents live?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: In the upper part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you build your new house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I built it in Tuk. That's the area. We call it Tuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When did you build that house, the new house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: The new house, I started building it somewhere in 1980, 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned the neighbourhood. Who were some of your neighbours in that neighbourhood around your new house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: My closest neighbours were Marija Papic, Pero Papic, then Dragan Papic further away, and Skoro, the three Skoro brothers, three, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: These were all your Croatian neighbours, I take it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: All Croatian, except further down, there was Ahmic Alija. He was my closest neighbour further down. Of the Muslims, further away, there were a few others, Sulejman Ahmic and his son Enver Ahmic with his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think, Alija Ahmic. Did he have a son by the name of Abdulah?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher at this time to show an exhibit to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, before you start pointing at everything, I just want to ask you a couple of questions, Mr. Ahmic. Did you have a chance to examine this exhibit before coming into court today?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall looking at a similar aerial map in which you placed some circles around houses that you could identify?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall having looked at something like this earlier, this picture, on an earlier occasion when you and I were talking, and you pointed out some of the houses that you could identify, like, your house and Papic's house, and we drew some circles around them. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did it here, but before that, I had no possibility to see it or to show anything or to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I understand. Now, could you look at the exhibit, which is now number Exhibit 75, and see if those are the circles that correspond to the circles that you placed on the map?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Circle 75, well, it's missing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think maybe you misunderstand my question. Let me ask you this: Do you see your house on the map?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What number is your house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Thirty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, is that the house that you said you built or started to build in 1980?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the house that I built, the new house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Alija Ahmic, whose son was Abdulah, as one of your neighbours, one of your Muslim neighbours. Do you see his house and, if so, what is the number of his house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, down here, number 38. This is his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned having lived close to some Croatian neighbours. I believe you mentioned Marija and Pero, for example. Do you see their houses marked and, if so, what letters or numbers were they given on this map?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Pero's house has the letter "H" here, and Marija's house is here shown under letter "I."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You also mentioned Ivo Papic or Dragan Papic's house. What letter or number, if any, corresponds or matches that house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is this house under letter "A," yes. This is Ivo Papic's house where Dragan Papic lived together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were a life-long resident of Ahmici and moved into your house, here number 37 on the map, in 1980. Could you describe for us the kinds of relationships you had with your Croatian neighbours at that time, let's say, between 1980 and 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: We were very close. We lived in peace. We would visit each other. I personally went to attend the party when Dragan Papic was leaving for the JNA service, when he was married. Marija would come. We really lived very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Ivo Papic house and, as a friend, be entertained in that house or be invited into that house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at Ivo Papic's house. He built my bathroom. He did all sorts of works. We were very good, and I would visit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You said, I think, that Ivo Papic lived in that house. Did you say, as well, that Dragan Papic lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ivo Papic lived on the ground floor, and Dragan Papic lived on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that Dragan Papic, at some point, went off to join the JNA. That would be the National Yugoslavian Army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? I didn't understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said that you attended a function at the Ivo Papic house when Dragan Papic was going to join the JNA. Tell us what the JNA is.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When Dragan Papic was leaving for his service to the Yugoslav People's Army when Yugoslavia existed, I was there. And when he had the wedding, I was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you also join the JNA or participate in the JNA yourself?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I served in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: When was that, about?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: That was in 1976. I joined in October 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to the early 1990s in Ahmici. Let me first ask you: Were you a member of the Territorial Defence at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what was the Territorial Defence in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in Ahmici existed for security reasons so that there would be no incidents flaring up. I joined the Territorial Defence because I was fired from the steel factory, and I was on hold until a next job would be found for me. And I decided to join the Territorial Defence because I thought, perhaps, they would help me with the new job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why were you fired from the steel factory?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Simply, we were put on hold, on a waiting list, sort of. There was not enough work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So it was a lay-off, basically?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know, the production had to be halted, and they couldn't keep paying our salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, originally, when you joined the Territorial Defence, were there joint patrols? That is to say, did the Croatians and the Muslims cooperate together in patrolling Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I was on patrol together with them, because my house is located next to the road, and we would go on patrol together. They would also give me weapons. I got it from Rafael Skoro. I got an M-48 machine gun, and I would surrender the weapon back to him when my patrol duty was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, this person who gave you the machine gun, was that a Croatian neighbour of yours or a Muslim neighbour of yours?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not the automatic machine gun that he issued to me. It was a rifle, an M-47, I think it was called, and it was issued to me by a Croatian by the name Rafael Skoro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And this was while there was cooperation and joint patrol between Croatians and Muslims in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when this cooperation ended?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did end, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, what happened, they simply -- well, Skoro Rafael simply said, "We cannot go on patrol together anymore. You go and join your people," and this is what happened. I left them and I would join my people and would go on guard duty together with them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, the Territorial Defence after the split, would you describe the Territorial Defence as an organised military operation or was it more of a neighbourhood watch?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, when we started with these guard duties, we didn't have weapons. Well, maybe a person here and there had a personal gun. We would go on guard, simply because of certain incidents. And sometimes it was not really guards, proper guard duty. We would sit down, play cards or play chess. That is how it looked like. As far as the organisation of the Territorial Defence is concerned, well, it comprised the citizens who were put on a waiting list, because there was no work for them. There was actually no special organisation involved, no real organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, at some point, was this Territorial Defence incorporated into the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I do not know when they were incorporated into the BiH army. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Without telling us when, do you know if, in fact, it happened, that there was this incorporation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that it did take place, but I do not know when this incorporation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did the transformation or change from Territorial Defence to being part of the BiH army create any changes at all in the way the patrols were done in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, it brought about no change. Everything remained as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now I want to direct your attention to the incident that occurred in Ahmici in October of 1992. Do you recall that at all?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you recall?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, just before this event took place, I was not at home. I was at Han Bila with my friends. In the evening, when I came home from my job, my wife told me that I should go on guard down to my house, because she said that the situation was no good or there could be problems around the bend. I was on guard duty that very evening. In the morning, I don't know when, I think it was around 5.30 in the morning when we were supposed to pray, a detonation, an explosion was heard, and shots started being fired. So the shots were fired. I personally do not know why, how, and what exactly was going on. I was just assigned this guard duty. Abdulah and myself were there together. Later on, Muris came in, that is his brother, and he told us that we should withdraw and that we should go to Ahmici. However, I had a wife and children in my house. I went there to wake them up. Actually, they were already awake, and they were asking me what was going on. I couldn't tell them what was going on. I just told them, "You get ready and I will take you up there." I did this. They took things with them, and I took them to the upper part of Ahmici. Afterwards, I came back. I went down to Sakib's stable, because this is how far we withdrew, how far we went to get away for the first time. Here I saw Sakib Ahmic. He was approaching us. At that time, Alija's stable was already on fire, and he asked me, "What is going on? Why is the stable on fire?" We couldn't answer him. He was very upset, and he went down to see Ivo Papic. While we were there, I heard, myself, shots being fired from the forest, from Dragan's house, from that direction, towards Mehmed's house. I didn't stay there for a long time. There was no order. You didn't know what to do. You just did whatever you thought was best, so I got away towards upper Ahmici. In the evening, Zasna, Mehmed's wife, got out with her children, and I guess her mother was with them as well. And she said that her house had been set on fire and that they barely managed to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I interrupt you just to clarify a couple of points, Mr. Ahmic? You said, I think, that evening you were on guard duty. Using Exhibit 75, which is that piece of paper next to you, and if you recall this, could you demonstrate or show where you were on guard duty when the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Here, under Abdulah's house, Alija's house, that is Abdulah's son's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That would be around House 38 as marked on this exhibit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, were you armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Once the shooting started, where did you go, if you could show us on that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I first went to my house. My wife and my children, I took them out. I told them to get away, to go to Upper Ahmici. Then I went out together with them. I took them to Upper Ahmici. That was next to Vlatko's house. And then I came back again to Sakib's stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, let's stop there for a moment. You mentioned Sakib. Were there two Sakibs in Ahmici, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were two Sakibs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Is the Sakib you're referring to here, is this the Sakib -- well, why don't you tell us which Sakib you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Sakib Biric. That's Biricini Sakib. That's how we called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was this Sakib related in any way to Abdulah; do you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, that is his uncle -- well, Sakib is Abdulah's uncle's father's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: In any event, some relationship to Abdulah?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were relatives, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, did you take your family at this time then to the house of your father and mother in Upper Ahmici where you used to live?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just escorted them to a point above Vlatko's house from where the Muslim houses start, and I told them to go ahead to Ahmici, to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Then you returned to Sakib's house. Could you show us where Sakib's house is, please?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't return to Sakib's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I returned as far as Sakib's stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you find that on the map for us?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Here -- no. No, let me see. Here. Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And that would be fairly close to that spot that's marked "X" on the map; is that correct? Just to the right of that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, just there. Exactly here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did you do or see when you got to that stable?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When I got to the stable, there were another two men there, another two neighbours who told me that Mehmed was inside with his wife and children, that there was fire around them and they couldn't get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned Mehmed. Do you see his house on Exhibit 75?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I do. Here it is marked with number 3 (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Go on. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When they said that Mehmed was inside and his wife and children and that they couldn't get out because of the shooting that was coming from Dragan Papic and Ivo Papic's house and from the woods, they were simply there. They had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you see firing coming from Papic Ivo's house directed at Mehmed's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I heard these two men saying to me that the fire was coming from down there, and I heard the fire but I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: After that, I withdrew to Upper Ahmici to look for my wife and children; however, they had gone further towards Vrhovine. So I stayed in Ahmici, in Upper Ahmici, on guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you mention that your family went to Upper Ahmici. Do you know if other families as well from that part of Ahmici, do you know if they also fled their homes and went to other areas of the village to avoid the shooting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are many of them. More than half the village fled to Vrhovine and Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you know what prompted this conflict in 1992 in Ahmici, either know it personally, by personal knowledge, or by what you've heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know anything about that, what it was that had provoked the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you understand happened?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about a barricade that had been set up on the main road to Vitez and Busovaca, that main road around the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I heard that there was a barricade. I wasn't connected to the barricade and I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you said your family went up to live in a home in Upper Ahmici. Did you then join them a short time later?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. They had left for Vrhovine, and later on, after some time, I don't know exactly how many days later, I went to fetch them and brought them back to Upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you remain in Upper Ahmici for a period of time with your family?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Gornji Ahmici. Afterwards, we returned home. I don't know when this was. But I didn't say, after this mess had happened, I forgot to mention that I went back and then, two days later, I dragged Halid, who was killed, myself and Mirsad Ahmic, we dragged him to Hodzija's mosque and his body was taken over by his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Tell us, who was Halid Pezer?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Halid Pezer was Omer Pezer's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How old was he?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Roughly, I would say, 18, 17. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you find his body?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: We found it behind Pjanics' house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: He was killed with a single bullet, I think from a sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you know when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know when, but I heard that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was this in connection with the incident you had described where the shooting had been taking place into Mehmed Ahmic's house, that incident?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no. It's not linked to that. He was killed over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was it the same day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: The same day, yes, when the shooting occurred. It was the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, after you joined your family in Upper Ahmici following this incident, I think you've indicated that you returned back to your house at some point later. Did you return with your family or without your family?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I returned home with my family, and on my way home, just above Pero's house, I was stopped by Dragan and Vinko as I was going home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you show us on the exhibit there in front of you the route you took with your family to go home on the day you were stopped by the Papics?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is where I was stopped by Dragan Papic and Vinko Vidovic. They told me that I should go to Slavko Skoro's to ask for permission and to be safe when I return home. However, I didn't do as they told me. I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, there is some markers there next to you. If you could take a red marker and just put an "X" at the approximate point on the exhibit where you were stopped by the Papics as you were going home. The usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's fine. That will do. Could you tell us again or tell us who was at that point when you arrived there with your family on your way home?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I only saw Simo near the bunker. The bunker had been made by my own building blocks and there was a machine gun there. I think it was an M-53, an old model.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You say there was a bunker there made from blocks taken from your house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And there was a machine gun of some sort behind those blocks?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Who was around that machine gun when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: There was Simo Vidovic, the son of Vinko Vidovic, who stopped me together with Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How was -- if you recall, how was Vinko Vidovic dressed? In civilian clothes or in uniform?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They were all in uniform. They were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What did Vinko Vidovic or Dragan Papic say to you as you approached them?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They told me that I should go and see Slavko Skoro to ask him for some sort of permission and security in order to be able to return to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you understand why you would need permission to return to your own home?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't understand at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you mention anything to Dragan Papic or the other man with him about having seen your blocks being used without your permission?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Why didn't you confront them about that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't dare. We, down there, were like convicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: What do you mean, "convicts"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: My own wife was afraid, when I was on guard duty just above the road, she was terrified that I went there, leaving them alone. She said, "We're alone here among them. They are wearing camouflage uniforms, carrying weapons, and showing off with those weapons." And simply we were there -- we didn't know what to do -- like detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you go home despite the fact that you were told you needed permission?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I went home, I spent the night. That night, I protected the windows in case they would throw anything inside; and in the morning, when we got up, Dragan Papic and Vinko Vidovic, I was sitting with my wife outside at a table in the yard, they came up to me. What their intention was, I don't know. I just know that Dragan had the fuse of a bomb because my wife asked him what it was, and he said it was a fuse for a bomb. And then Vinko Vidovic showed me a card indicating that he was a member of a special unit, the Jokers, and they were based in the Bungalow. Then they asked us, "Why don't you monkeys," as they said, "surrender? What do they think?" And my answer was "I don't know anything" because I wasn't interested in any of it. Later, I moved my wife from there for her safety as well as the children to Bistricak and I moved above the road among my people to continue keeping watch duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mention that Dragan Papic, when he visited you the next morning, had a bomb fuse. What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It looked like a -- like a stick, about this size (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You mention that Vinko Vidovic talked about some sort of special unit at the Bungalow. Did he show you anything to verify that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: He showed me -- I didn't ask him to show me anything. He showed me a card that looked like an ID card. I didn't take it into my hands, but he himself told me that he belonged to a special unit, the unit called Jokers in the Bungalow or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did they say anything else to you in addition to, "Why don't you monkeys surrender?" that you can recall? I'm not asking you word for word. That would be, I think, impossible, but just the general idea of what they told you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall them saying anything about having protected your house from attack during the incident that you had described earlier?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When they approached, then they said to me that they had tried, that their HVO soldiers had tried to break into my house, and Dragan Papic personally told me that it was a Croatian house, "Don't touch it," because when I arrived, I could see the imprint of soldiers' boots on the door when they had tried to break in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, I think -- and this, I think, will be the last question, with the permission of the Court, if this is the time to stop. You left the next day from your house after this visit from Mr. Papic and Mr. Vidovic. Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I left because I didn't feel safe. I wasn't sure that they wouldn't do something to me, throw a bomb or something, and so we had to leave our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be an appropriate time to stop, if the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I gather you have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I will have questions that will deal then with the attack on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 4.20 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of August, 1998, at 9.30 a.m.
